prompt: Let $x$ and $y$ be elements of a finite $p$-group $P$ and let $z = [x, y]$ be the commutator $x^{-1}y^{-1}xy$ of $x$ and $y$. Suppose that $x$ lies in every normal subgroup of $P$ which contains $z$. Prove that $x = 1$.
answer: Induction on $|P|$: pass to $P/Z$ with $Z$ a central subgroup of order $p$; by induction $x\in Z$, so $z=[x,y]=1$, and then $x$ lies in the normal subgroup $1$.

solutions.title: Induction modulo a central subgroup
solutions.body:
Induct on $|P|$; the case $|P|=1$ is trivial. Let $|P|>1$. The center of a nontrivial $p$-group is nontrivial, so $P$ has a central subgroup $Z$ of order $p$. Let $\bar P=P/Z$ and write bars for images; then $\bar z=[\bar x,\bar y]$.

The hypothesis passes to $\bar P$: if $\bar M\trianglelefteq\bar P$ contains $\bar z$, its full preimage $M$ is normal in $P$ and contains $z$, so $x\in M$ and $\bar x\in\bar M$. By induction ($|\bar P|<|P|$), $\bar x=1$, i.e. $x\in Z$.

Now $x$ is central, so $z=[x,y]=1$. The trivial subgroup is normal and contains $z$, so by hypothesis $x\in\langle1\rangle$, i.e. $x=1$. ∎

prompt:
Let $K[x]$ be a polynomial ring over the field $K$ and let $R$ be the subring of $K[x]$ consisting of all polynomials whose $x$-coefficient is equal to $0$. Thus a typical element of $R$ has the form
$$a_0 + a_2x^2 + a_3x^3 + \cdots + a_nx^n$$
with $a_i \in K$. Show that the principal ideal $(x^2) = x^2R$ is a primary ideal of $R$ which is not equal to a power of its radical.
answer: $Q=x^2R$ consists of the elements of $R$ with no $x^3$ term and zero constant term; $\sqrt Q=P=x^2R+x^3R$ (constant term $0$). $P\supsetneq Q\supsetneq P^2$ (since $x^3\in P\setminus Q$, $x^2\in Q\setminus P^2$), and a direct computation with constant terms shows $Q$ is primary.

solutions.title: Explicit description of the ideals
solutions.body:
Note $R=K\oplus x^2K[x]$ and
$$Q=x^2R=\{a_2x^2+a_4x^4+a_5x^5+\cdots\}$$
(elements of $R$ with zero constant term and zero $x^3$-coefficient), since $x^2(c_0+c_2x^2+c_3x^3+\cdots)=c_0x^2+c_2x^4+c_3x^5+\cdots$. Let
$$P=\{f\in R: f(0)=0\}=\{a_2x^2+a_3x^3+\cdots\}.$$
$P$ is the kernel of $R\to K$, $f\mapsto f(0)$, so it is a maximal ideal.

**$\sqrt Q=P$.** If $f\in R$ and $f^k\in Q$, then $f(0)^k=0$, so $f\in P$. Conversely if $f\in P$ then $f^2\in x^4K[x]\subseteq Q$. So $\sqrt Q=P$.

**$Q$ is primary.** Let $g,h\in R$ with $gh\in Q$ and $g\notin P$, i.e. $c_0=g(0)\ne0$. Write $g=c_0+c_2x^2+c_3x^3+\cdots$, $h=d_0+d_2x^2+d_3x^3+\cdots$. Then
$$gh=c_0d_0+(c_0d_2+c_2d_0)x^2+(c_0d_3+c_3d_0)x^3+\cdots .$$
$gh\in Q$ gives $c_0d_0=0$, so $d_0=0$, and then $c_0d_3=0$, so $d_3=0$. Thus $h\in Q$. Hence whenever $gh\in Q$, either $h\in Q$ or $g\in P=\sqrt Q$: $Q$ is primary (with radical $P$).

**$Q$ is not a power of $P$.** $P^1=P\ne Q$ since $x^3\in P\setminus Q$. Every product of two elements of $P$ lies in $x^4K[x]$, so $P^n\subseteq P^2\subseteq x^4K[x]$ for $n\ge2$, while $x^2\in Q\setminus x^4K[x]$. So $Q\neq P^n$ for all $n\ge1$ (and $Q\ne P^0=R$). ∎

prompt:
Let $E$ be a finite degree field extension of the rationals $\mathbb{Q}$ and suppose that $f(x)$ is a monic irreducible polynomial in $E[x]$.

(i) Show that there exists a unique monic irreducible polynomial $g(x) \in \mathbb{Q}[x]$ such that $f(x)$ divides $g(x)$ in $E[x]$.

(ii) Let $g(x)$ be as above. If $E$ is a splitting field over $\mathbb{Q}$ for some polynomial in $\mathbb{Q}[x]$, show that the degree of $f(x)$ divides the degree of $g(x)$.

(iii) Give an example to show that the degree of $f(x)$ need not divide the degree of $g(x)$ in general.
answer: (i) $g$ is the minimal polynomial over $\mathbb Q$ of a root $\alpha$ of $f$. (ii) If $E/\mathbb Q$ is Galois, $g$ is the product of the distinct $\mathrm{Gal}(E/\mathbb Q)$-conjugates of $f$, all of degree $\deg f$. (iii) $E=\mathbb Q(\sqrt[3]2)$, $f$ the minimal polynomial of $\omega\sqrt[3]2$ over $E$ (degree 2), $g=x^3-2$.

solutions.title: Minimal polynomials and Galois conjugates
solutions.body:
**(i)** Let $\alpha$ be a root of $f$ in an extension of $E$. Then $|E[\alpha]:\mathbb Q|=|E[\alpha]:E|\,|E:\mathbb Q|<\infty$, so $\alpha$ is algebraic over $\mathbb Q$; let $g$ be its minimal polynomial over $\mathbb Q$. Since $f$ is the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$ over $E$ and $g(\alpha)=0$, $f\mid g$ in $E[x]$.

Uniqueness: if $h\in\mathbb Q[x]$ is monic irreducible with $f\mid h$, then $h(\alpha)=0$, so $g\mid h$ in $\mathbb Q[x]$; irreducibility and monicity of $h$ force $h=g$.

**(ii)** If $E$ is a splitting field over $\mathbb Q$, then $E/\mathbb Q$ is Galois (characteristic $0$); let $G=\mathrm{Gal}(E/\mathbb Q)$ act on $E[x]$ coefficientwise. Each $f^\sigma$ is monic irreducible in $E[x]$ of degree $\deg f$, and $f^\sigma\mid g^\sigma=g$. Let $f=f_1,\dots,f_k$ be the distinct conjugates $f^\sigma$ and $h=f_1\cdots f_k$. $G$ permutes the $f_i$, so $h$ is $G$-invariant and $h\in E^G[x]=\mathbb Q[x]$. The $f_i$ are distinct monic irreducibles dividing $g$, so $h\mid g$; and $h(\alpha)=0$, so $g\mid h$. Both are monic, so $g=h$ and $\deg g=k\deg f$.

**(iii)** Let $E=\mathbb Q(\sqrt[3]2)\subset\mathbb R$, which is not normal over $\mathbb Q$. Let $\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}$ and $\beta=\omega\sqrt[3]2$. Then $E[\beta]=E[\omega]$ has degree $2$ over $E$ ($\omega\notin\mathbb R$, and $\omega^2+\omega+1=0$), so the minimal polynomial $f$ of $\beta$ over $E$ has degree $2$; explicitly $f=(x-\omega\sqrt[3]2)(x-\omega^2\sqrt[3]2)=x^2+\sqrt[3]2\,x+\sqrt[3]4$. The unique $g$ of (i) is the minimal polynomial of $\beta$ over $\mathbb Q$, namely $x^3-2$ (irreducible by Eisenstein at $2$). Indeed $x^3-2=(x-\sqrt[3]2)f(x)$, and $2\nmid3$. ∎

prompt:
Let $V$ be a finite dimensional vector space over a field $K$ and let $B\colon V \times V \to K$ be a bilinear form. Suppose that for all $x, y \in V$ we have $B(x, y) = 0$ if and only if $B(y, x) = 0$.

(i) If $v, w \in V$ with $B(v, v) \neq 0$, prove that $B(v, w) = B(w, v)$.

(ii) Deduce that either $B$ is symmetric or $B(v, v) = 0$ for all $v \in V$.
answer: (i) Apply the hypothesis to $v$ and $u=w-kv$ with $k=B(v,w)/B(v,v)$. (ii) If $B(v,v)\ne0$ for some $v$, write $V=Kv\oplus v^\perp$ and use (i) with $v$ or $v+x$ to get symmetry on $v^\perp$.

solutions.title: Orthogonal projection
solutions.body:
**(i)** Let $k=B(v,w)B(v,v)^{-1}$ and $u=w-kv$. Then $B(v,u)=B(v,w)-kB(v,v)=0$, so by hypothesis $B(u,v)=0$, i.e. $B(w,v)=kB(v,v)=B(v,w)$.

**(ii)** Suppose $B(v,v)\ne0$ for some $v$. Let $W=\{w: B(v,w)=0\}$, which by hypothesis also equals $\{w:B(w,v)=0\}$. $W$ is the kernel of the nonzero functional $w\mapsto B(v,w)$ (nonzero at $v$), so $V=Kv\oplus W$.

Let $x,y\in W$. If $B(x,x)\ne0$, then $B(x,y)=B(y,x)$ by (i). If $B(x,x)=0$, then
$$B(v+x,v+x)=B(v,v)+B(v,x)+B(x,v)+B(x,x)=B(v,v)\ne0,$$
so by (i), using $B(v,y)=B(y,v)=0$,
$$B(x,y)=B(v+x,y)=B(y,v+x)=B(y,x).$$
So $B$ is symmetric on $W$. Also $B(v,w)=B(w,v)=0$ for $w\in W$ and trivially $B(v,v)=B(v,v)$. By bilinearity $B$ is symmetric on $V=Kv\oplus W$.

So if $B$ is not symmetric, $B(v,v)=0$ for every $v$ (and then $B$ is alternating). ∎

prompt:
Let $G$ be the multiplicative group of all $2 \times 2$ matrices over the integers $\mathbb{Z}$ whose determinant is equal to $1$. Notice that $G$ acts by right multiplication on the set $\Omega$ of all 1-dimensional subspaces of the 2-dimensional row space $\mathbb{Q}^2$ over the rational numbers $\mathbb{Q}$.

(i) Find all elements of $G$ which act trivially, that is which fix every element of $\Omega$.

(ii) Prove that $G$ acts transitively. In other words, show that $\Omega$ is an orbit under the action of $G$.
answer: (i) Only $\pm I$. (ii) Each line contains a primitive vector $(r,s)$, $\gcd(r,s)=1$; choose $x,y$ with $rx-sy=1$, then $g=\begin{pmatrix}r&s\\y&x\end{pmatrix}\in G$ sends $\mathbb Q(1,0)$ to $\mathbb Q(r,s)$.

solutions.title: Test vectors and Bézout
solutions.body:
**(i)** Let $g=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$ act trivially. Then $(1,0)g=(a,b)\in\mathbb Q(1,0)$ gives $b=0$; $(0,1)g=(c,d)\in\mathbb Q(0,1)$ gives $c=0$; and $(1,1)g=(a,d)\in\mathbb Q(1,1)$ gives $a=d$. Then $\det g=a^2=1$, so $g=\pm I$. Conversely $\pm I$ send every vector to $\pm$ itself, so they fix every line. The kernel of the action is $\{\pm I\}$.

**(ii)** We show every line $\ell\in\Omega$ lies in the orbit of $\mathbb Q(1,0)$. Take $0\ne(u,v)\in\ell$; multiplying by a common denominator and dividing by the gcd of the numerators, $\ell$ contains a vector $(r,s)\in\mathbb Z^2$ with $\gcd(r,s)=1$. By Bézout there are integers $x,y$ with $rx-sy=1$. Put
$$g=\begin{pmatrix}r&s\\y&x\end{pmatrix},\qquad \det g=rx-sy=1,$$
so $g\in G$, and $(1,0)g=(r,s)$. Hence $(\mathbb Q(1,0))g=\ell$, and the action is transitive. ∎
